  Negative Appraisals: Mistrust: People can't be trusted, Emotional Numbness: I feel dead inside, Survival Guilt: I feel guilty for surviving when others did not

Vignette:
The morning the barometer dropped without warning, Minh and his younger brother, Dat, were thirty miles off the coast of Monterey, hauling lines through choppy water. The sky bruised purple, and the wind took the wheelhouse before Minh could secure the winch. He watched Dat slip over the gunwale, the deck slick with rain and diesel, reaching out until his fingers brushed only air. When the coast guard boat finally found Dat’s jacket tangled in the kelp, Minh was left on the returning vessel with empty hands and a chest that wouldn’t stop seizing. He had come to believe that the storm had pulled his brother under so he could go, that the sea had made a bargain he never agreed to. Weeks later, the first time the harbor bell rang at dusk, Minh’s hands locked onto the cabin doorframe until his knuckles turned white. His heart hammered against his ribs, and a hot wave of shame rolled through him, as though he were still standing where the deck had given way. He stopped sleeping through the night. By the second month, he would lie on his side with his eyes open, listening to the ceiling fan click, counting the spaces between his breaths until dawn. What frightened him most was not the dark, but the quiet moments when his mind would drift backward and he felt it again—the sickening lurch in his stomach, the sudden spike of anger at the sky, the horror that settled in his throat like a stone. He would freeze mid-stride when the tide pools turned black, his gaze fixed on the horizon, waiting for the ghost of a radio call that never came. He had come to believe that people could not be trusted to keep him safe. When the new deckhand, a young man from the coastal community, offered to check the winch cable for him, Minh turned away, telling himself that attention would slip again, that reliance only left you exposed. He stopped inviting his wife, Linh, to sit with him on the deck after the sun went down. Instead, he moved through the boat like a shadow, his chest tight, his feelings drained until even the smell of her coffee felt distant. He felt dead inside, a hollow space where his grief used to sit. When he looked at Dat’s empty bunk, he was certain it was his fault for breathing that morning, for staying dry while Dat drowned. The habits hardened over months. He avoided the marine radio during squalls, changed routes when the water looked too gray, and let the vessel drift past known shoals rather than risk the sudden shifts that followed. On the boat, where the salt air usually grounded him, the sudden crack of a winch rope now sent a jolt straight to his jaw, his shoulders curling inward as if expecting the deck to tilt. His wife noticed the quiet distance, how he flinched when the diesel engine caught, how he no longer answered her questions about the catch or the season. He told himself that staying away from the harbor was the only way to keep his head steady, but the distance between him and Linh grew with every tide he refused to run. What finally brought him to the clinic was a morning when he stood at the edge of the pier, watching the fog roll in, and found his hands shaking so badly he could not unclasp his coat. He came because the quiet inside him no longer felt like protection, because he was tired of waking up before the alarm, and because he was hoping, however faintly, to sit through a dinner with Linh without bracing for the storm that never came.
